title: Offering Alternatives & Counter-Proposals
summary: Turn a no into a way forward: offer options (*one option would be to…*, *alternatively…*), suggest tentatively with past forms (*What if we added…?*, *Would it help if I…?*), set conditions (*provided / as long as* + present) and build a counter-proposal on the other person's plan instead of replacing it.
canDo: Present two or three options and recommend one, with *one option would be to*, *alternatively* and *rather than*.
Make tentative suggestions with *What if we + past?*, *Would it help if I + past?* and *How about + -ing?*
Set conditions with *provided (that)* and *as long as* + present simple.
Hear and say the weak forms of *could*, *or* and *as*, and link *what if* into one beat.

focus.grammar: What if / Would it help if + past simple (tentative suggestion) · How about + -ing · one option would be to + verb · rather than / instead of + -ing · provided (that) / as long as + present simple for the future · suggest + -ing / that-clause
focus.lexis: one option would be to, alternatively, what if we, how about, would it help if, rather than, as long as, provided (that), that could work, a phased approach, a fallback, meet someone halfway, put something to someone
focus.afh: weak forms: could /kəd/, or /ɚ/ · /ə/, as /əz/ (as long as) · linking what if /wʌt̬‿ˈɪf/ · alTERnative (stress on the second syllable)

warmup: Think of a time when someone said no to your idea and then offered something else. Did the alternative feel like a real offer or like a polite way to end the conversation? What made the difference?

discovery.intro: Before the meeting, Priya replies to Ryan's options email. She wants to change his plan without rejecting it.
discovery.speaker: priya
discovery.text: Ryan, I'd go with option one too, but {{what if we added}} an invoice-number filter to the basic search? {{Rather than}} waiting until July, customers {{would get}} the search they use most on day one. It would take Alex about three days, {{provided}} we {{keep}} it to that one filter. {{Would it help if}} I {{mocked}} it up today, so Helen can see it tomorrow? Priya

organizer.title: How Priya builds her counter-proposal
organizer.prompt: Name the function of each part: suggestion, benefit, condition or offer.
rows: What if we added an invoice-number filter to the basic search?
Customers would get the search they use most on day one.
…provided we keep it to that one filter.
Would it help if I mocked it up today?
organizer.explain: A strong counter-proposal agrees first, then suggests a change, shows the benefit, limits the risk with a condition and offers effort.

questions.q: Priya writes *What if we added a filter?* and *Would it help if I mocked it up today?* The verbs are past (*added*, *mocked*), but the actions are in the future. What do the past forms do here? How would *What if we add a filter?* sound different?
questions.model: The past forms do not refer to the past: they make the suggestion hypothetical, a possibility to consider rather than a plan already decided. That distance makes the counter-proposal tentative and easy to turn down without conflict. *What if we add a filter?* is also correct, but it sounds more direct, closer to a plan that has been decided. It is the same distance that the Second Conditional creates.
criteria: You said the past forms do not refer to past time.
You said they make the suggestion hypothetical and softer, easy to turn down.
You said the present (*what if we add*) sounds more direct, closer to a decision.

questions.q: Write the pattern that follows each of these: *what if*, *would it help if*, *how about*, *rather than*, *provided (that)*. Which one takes a present form even though it refers to the future?

signals.label: what if / would it help if + past

questions.model: *What if* + subject + past simple (or the present, which is more direct). *Would it help if* + subject + past simple. *How about* + -ing or a noun (*how about adding just the invoice filter?*). *Rather than* + bare infinitive or -ing (*rather than wait / waiting until July*). *Provided (that)* and *as long as* + present simple, even when they refer to the future: *provided we keep it to one filter*, never *provided we will keep*.
criteria: You gave *what if* / *would it help if* + past simple and *how about* + -ing.
You said *provided / as long as* take the present for the future, never *will*.

questions.q: Priya changes part of Ryan's plan, but she never writes *no* or *I disagree*. How does she make the counter-proposal easy to accept? What does *Would it help if I mocked it up today* add?
questions.model: She starts by agreeing (*I'd go with option one too*), then adds her idea as a hypothetical question, so Ryan can say no without losing face. She gives a benefit for the customers (*the search they use most on day one*), a cost (*about three days*) and a condition that limits the risk (*that one filter*). The offer to mock it up turns her idea into her own work: she takes on the effort, and Helen gets something concrete to look at. A counter-proposal that builds on the other person's plan and offers effort is much easier to accept than a rival plan.
criteria: You said she agrees first and builds on Ryan's plan instead of replacing it.
You mentioned the benefit, the cost and the condition that limits the risk.
You said the offer to mock it up adds her own effort and something concrete for Helen.

points: Offer alternatives as options, not orders: *one option would be to…*, *alternatively, we could…*, *rather than X, we could Y*. Recommend one, and keep another as a fallback.
Past forms after *what if* and *would it help if* make a suggestion hypothetical and easy to discuss: *What if we added a filter?* is softer than *What if we add a filter?*
A good counter-proposal builds on the other plan: agree first, add your change, give the benefit and the cost, set a condition, offer your effort.
After *provided (that)*, *as long as* and *unless*, use the present for the future: *provided we keep it small*, never *provided we will keep*.
formulas: One option would be to + verb · Alternatively, we could + verb
What if / Would it help if + subject + past simple? · How about + -ing?
Rather than + verb / -ing · provided (that) / as long as + present simple
rule.note: Spanish *¿y si añadimos un filtro?* uses the present, and English accepts *what if we add…?* too; the past (*what if we added…?*) is the more diplomatic choice. And Spanish *sugerir que añadamos* is *suggest (that) we add* or *suggest adding*, never *suggest us to add*.

phonetics.intro: Las propuestas se construyen con palabras funcionales que casi no se oyen: *could* /kəd/, *or* /ə(r)/, *as* /əz/. Si las dices con vocal plena, la propuesta suena insistente, como una exigencia. Débiles, suenan a sugerencia. *What if* es un caso aparte: dos palabras que se pronuncian como una sola.

items.meaning: a possibility or a tentative suggestion

alerts.text: *Could* es /kəd/: «kəd», con schwa. No «kuld» ni «kud» con u plena.
La l de *could*, *would* y *should* nunca suena, ni en la forma fuerte: *could* fuerte es /kʊd/, «kud».
Es fuerte al final o en negativa: *Yes, we could* /kʊd/; *we couldn't* /ˈkʊd.ənt/.

example.speaker: alex
example.text: We could try a filter by invoice number.

alerts.text: *Or* se reduce a /ɚ/ (US) o /ə/ (UK): «ər», casi una sola vocal. No «OR» con o plena.
En UK, delante de vocal reaparece la r: *July or August* «dyu-LAI-ə-RÓO-gəst».
Cuando *or* contrasta dos opciones con énfasis (*now, OR in July?*), recupera la vocal plena: /ɔːr/.

example.speaker: oliver
example.text: We could run the check this week or next.
example.tts: We [could](/kəd/) run the check this week [or](/ə/) next.

alerts.text: Los dos *as* son /əz/: «əz», con schwa y z sonora. Solo *long* lleva acento.
*Long as* se une: «LÓ-ŋəz». La ng es /ŋ/, como la n de *tengo*: no añadas una g fuerte.
*Long*: US /ɔː/, una o abierta y larga; UK /ɒ/, breve y redondeada.

example.speaker: oliver
example.text: That could work, as long as we keep it small.
example.tts: That [could](/kəd/) work, [as](/əz/) long [as](/əz/) we keep it small.

items.meaning: introduces a suggestion or an imagined situation

alerts.text: En EE. UU., la t de *what* entre vocales suena como una r simple: «ua-RIF». En Reino Unido, t suave: «uo-TIF».
Dos palabras, un solo golpe: la t se une a *if* sin pausa. En *What if we added…?* la frase sigue sin cortes.
Sola, el acento cae en *if*: «ua-RIF?». Dentro de la pregunta, el acento principal pasa al verbo: *what if we ADDed a filter?*

alerts.text: Acento en la segunda sílaba: al-TER-na-tive. El español «alternativa» lo lleva en TI.
En TER, /ɜː/ es una vocal central y larga, ni e ni a; en UK, sin r. La tercera sílaba es schwa: «nə».
En EE. UU., la t final entre vocales es una r simple: «-nə-riv». La v final es /v/, no f.

l1.title: Suggest + object + to
l1.text: Spanish *te sugiero que* has no direct copy. Use *suggest* + -ing, or *suggest (that)* + subject + base form.
l1.wrong: I suggest you to add a filter.
l1.right: I suggest adding a filter. / I suggest (that) you add a filter.

l1.title: Instead of + base form
l1.text: *Instead of* is a preposition, so the verb takes -ing.
l1.wrong: Instead of move go-live, we could add the search in July.
l1.right: Instead of moving go-live, we could add the search in July.

l1.title: Will after provided
l1.text: After *provided (that)*, *as long as* and *unless*, use the present for the future, as after *if*.
l1.wrong: Provided we will keep it small, it could work.
l1.right: Provided we keep it small, it could work.

l1.title: Propose you something
l1.text: Spanish *le proponemos un enfoque* puts the person first. English *propose* takes the thing; the person goes after *to*, or disappears.
l1.wrong: We propose you a phased approach.

l1.title: How about + base form
l1.text: *About* is a preposition, so the verb takes -ing.
l1.wrong: How about add just the invoice filter?
l1.right: How about adding just the invoice filter?

task.title: A counter-proposal that builds on the other plan
task.scenario: Help-center project, one week before launch. After your voice message, Laura (head of support) came back with a counter-proposal: at least one video at launch, for password resets, which are a third of her team's tickets. A video can't be ready in a week. Your alternative: an illustrated step-by-step guide for password resets at launch (about two days of work for your designer), and three short videos in phase two, provided her team writes the scripts by the end of June. Write your reply.
task.brief: Build a counter-proposal on Laura's idea: agree first, suggest tentatively, give benefit and cost, set a condition, offer your effort.
steps: Agree with the part of her proposal you can accept.
Suggest your alternative with *what if we* + past or *one option would be to*.
Give the benefit for customers and the cost in time.
Set a condition with *provided (that)* or *as long as* + present.
Offer your own effort with *would it help if I* + past.

chunks.label: agreement first
chunks.re: \b(i agree|you're right|good point|that makes sense|i'd go with)\b

chunks.label: tentative suggestion
chunks.re: \bwhat if (we|i)\s+\w+ed\b|\bwhat if (we|i)\s+(made|sent|wrote|put|built|took|gave|did|ran|got|kept|began)\b|\bone option would be to\b|\bhow about\s+\w+ing\b

chunks.label: offer of effort
chunks.re: \bwould it help if (i|we)\b|\bi('d| would) be happy to\b|\bi can send\b

extra.title: Extra: the formal proposal for the steering committee
extra.brief: Turn your counter-proposal into one formal sentence: *As an alternative, we would propose…*, with the phased plan and a condition with *provided that*.
keywords: to follow in the second phase

parts.speaker: alex
parts.text: Hi Laura, thanks for coming back to me so quickly. {{I agree that}} password resets are the place to start: they're a third of your tickets. A video can't be ready in a week, though, so {{what if we}} launched with an illustrated step-by-step guide {{instead}}? {{Rather than}} a rushed video, {{customers would get}} clear screenshots on day one, and {{it would take}} our designer about two days. We could then produce three short videos for {{phase two}}, {{provided}} your team writes the scripts by the end of June. {{Would it help if I}} sent you a draft of the guide on Monday? Best, Alex
parts.label: Counter-proposal to a colleague (neutral email)
notes: *I agree that password resets are the place to start*: Alex accepts the core of Laura's idea before changing it.
*What if we launched with… instead?*: past simple after *what if*, so the alternative is offered, not imposed.
*Customers would get clear screenshots on day one* and *it would take our designer about two days*: the benefit and the cost, with *would*.
*Provided your team writes the scripts by the end of June*: a condition with the present for the future; it also gives Laura a role in phase two.
*Would it help if I sent you a draft on Monday?*: Alex offers his own effort and something concrete to react to.
parts.tts: Hi Laura, thanks [for](/fəɹ/) coming back to me so quickly. I agree that password resets are the place to start: they're a third [of](/əv/) your tickets. A video can't be ready in a week, though, so what if we launched with an illustrated step-by-step guide instead? Rather than a rushed video, customers [would](/wəd/) get clear screenshots on day one, [and](/ənd/) it [would](/wəd/) take our designer about two days. We [could](/kəd/) then produce three short videos [for](/fəɹ/) phase two, provided your team writes the scripts by the end [of](/əv/) June. [Would](/wəd/) it help if I sent you a draft [of](/əv/) the guide on Monday? Best, Alex

parts.speaker: emma
parts.text: {{As an alternative}}, {{we would propose}} an illustrated guide at launch, with three video tutorials {{to follow in the second phase}}, {{provided that}} the scripts {{are received by}} 30 June.
parts.tts: [As](/əz/) an alternative, we [would](/wəd/) propose an illustrated guide [at](/ət/) launch, with three video tutorials to follow in the second phase, provided that the scripts are received by the thirtieth [of](/əv/) June.
parts.label: The formal proposal (committee style)
notes: *As an alternative, we would propose*: the formal frame for a counter-proposal.

selfCheck.text: ¿Laura siente que mejoraste su idea o que la sustituiste por la tuya? Copia la frase en la que reconoces lo que ella tiene razón.
¿Tus propuestas suenan a opción (*what if we launched*, *one option would be to*) y no a orden (*we will do a guide*)? ¿Evitaste el tono de chat (*how about we just…*, *way easier*)?
¿*What if* y *would it help if* van con pasado, *how about* e *instead of* con -ing, y *provided / as long as* con presente (no *will*)?
¿Escribiste *suggest you to*, *propose you*, *instead of + infinitivo* o *provided we will*? Debe ser *suggest adding / that you add*, *propose a guide*, *instead of moving* y *provided we keep*.
